beats.narration_text: This is Aravind Ravi's week one explainer, read by a synthetic voice.

show.event: colophon: INFO 7375 · Week 1 · Randomness and first prompts · Aravind Ravi

lines: Why softmax code subtracts the biggest score,
and why the probabilities don't change
meta: INFO 7375 · Week 1 · Randomness and first prompts · Aravind Ravi

shot.decision: FormACard, not Manim: Gate A (static_scene_check) rejects a text-only Manim card as 'shapes never change', and adding a shape to pass it would be decoration.

qc.sparse_reason: Title card: a centred typographic card (FormACard) with deliberate negative space; the reviewer asked for a plain title card.

beats.narration_text: Softmax code subtracts the biggest score before it does anything else. I asked Claude Code to run the chapter's code both ways. Its answer: the weights differ, but the probabilities are identical to fifteen decimal places. Let's see why, and where it stops working.

show.event: the three verbatim reply lines type in
terracotta underline + tag 'claim — checked later' (paid off in B04)

reply_lines: - With max subtraction: [0.135, 0.368, 1.000] (smaller, more manageable numbers)
Final probabilities are identical to 15 decimal places.
beats.prompt_text: Run lessons/01-randomness-and-first-prompts/code/main.py and show me what probabilities([1, 2, 3]) returns. Then compute the same distribution without subtracting the max, and print both sets of intermediate weights side by side.

beats.narration_text: Here's the whole idea in one breath. Subtracting the biggest score changes the arithmetic, but none of the final probabilities. It's there for one reason: so the computer can finish the math without overflowing.

show.event: types 'Subtracting the biggest score changes the answer.'

props.text:
Subtracting the biggest score changes the answer.
The final probabilities stay the same.
It keeps the exponentials small enough to compute.

beats.motion_claim: The writer types the common misreading (the trick changes the answer) and corrects it: it changes the arithmetic, not the probabilities.

qc.sparse_reason: Hesitant-writer overview: the text accumulates token by token, so mid-beat frames are mostly page colour by design (the case named in final_frame_check.py).

beats.narration_text: Here's the rule. Raise e to each score, then divide by the total, so every result is positive and they all sum to one. Our input is three scores: one, two, and three. I picked those by hand; no model produced them. Temperature stays at one for this whole video, so only one thing moves.

show.event: three score chips 1 · 2 · 3 and T = 1 appear under the formula

qc.sparse_reason: The formula is held alone and large while the narration explains it; the input chips arrive on 'one, two, and three', after the mid-beat sample.

beats.narration_text: The direct route first. E to the one, two, and three gives about two point seven, seven point four, and twenty point one. Together, thirty point one nine. Divide each by that total: zero point oh nine, zero point two four, zero point six seven. The biggest score takes about two thirds.

show.event: B02's chips travel into the score column
x climbs 0→z with exp(x) beside it (true at every frame)
sum box; weights build a stacked bar at true relative widths (2.718 : 7.389 : 20.086)
the stack squashes to unit width; labels become 0.0900 / 0.2447 / 0.6652

shot.visual_intent: Left half of frame only — the right half is reserved (empty, labelled nothing) for B04's shifted column.

beats.narration_text: Now the route the code actually takes. Subtract the biggest score, three, from every entry: minus two, minus one, zero. Every weight changes, and the total drops from thirty to one and a half. Divide anyway, and the probabilities land on the same three values. Equal in exact math. On the computer, they agree to fifteen decimal places.

show.event: chips move onto a number line; brackets show gaps of 1 and 1
the whole line slides left by 3; the gap labels stay 1 and 1
shifted weights form a tiny stack at the same scale (sum 1.503 vs 30.193)
the tiny stack stretches to unit width and lands exactly on B03's unit bar
footnote: Claude's '15 decimal places' vs recorded 1.1 × 10⁻¹⁶, bit-identical False

shot.visual_intent: Side-by-side comparison, both columns held ≥2 s after the bars match.

beats.narration_text: Why is that allowed? Call the biggest score m. Subtracting m splits every weight into e to the z, times e to the minus m. That same factor sits in the top and the bottom of the fraction, so it cancels, and you're back at the original formula. The shift changes the weights. It can't change their ratios.

show.event: struck factors leave; the fraction collapses to exp(z_i)/Σexp(z_j)

beats.narration_text: A prediction, before the reason anyone bothers. Two scores, both a thousand. What probabilities should they get? And what happens on the direct route, when Python has to compute e to the thousand? Commit to both answers.

show.event: 'Predict first.' + the question on two balanced lines

qc.sparse_reason: Predict card: the question sits alone on the page so the viewer can think; the only motion is the countdown ring.

beats.narration_text: Equal scores, equal chances: one half each. The shifted route gets there in three steps. Subtract a thousand, get zeros; e to the zero is one; one over two. The direct route never arrives. E to the thousand is larger than any float can hold, and Python stops with an overflow error. The thousand carried no information. Only the difference did.

show.event: recorded sweep: x and exp(x) climb a log axis toward the largest float

shot.visual_intent: Error text must be pasted from the student's own run, not retyped from this sheet.

beats.narration_text: Here's what the subtraction doesn't buy. Try zero and minus a thousand. The small weight is e to the minus thousand: a real, positive number, but too small for a float, so it rounds to zero. The function reports a probability of exactly zero for an outcome the math says is possible. The shift prevents overflow. It doesn't prevent underflow.

show.event: recorded sweep: exp(−x) falls, losing digits (…4.2e-322, 1e-323, 5e-324) to 0.0

shot.visual_intent: The boundary beat. Recorded output from the student's run; the 10^−434 figure is labelled as computed, not printed.

beats.narration_text: So here's what to take away. Subtracting the max changes every intermediate weight and none of the final probabilities, because the shared factor cancels. It exists so large scores don't overflow. It doesn't stop tiny weights from underflowing to zero, and it never checks whether the winning score deserves to win.
takeaways: 0.0900, 0.2447, 0.6652 either way: the shared factor cancels
the top score gets the most probability, deserved or not

beats.narration_text: Your turn: Here is my softmax function: paste your code. Don't fix it, and don't tell me whether it's correct. Give me one finite input where subtracting the max still doesn't protect me, predict exactly what my function returns for it, and give me the one line I'd run to check. It holds back the fix and the verdict. Run that line yourself: the prediction is a hypothesis until your terminal agrees.
